hints: Focus on how oxidising strength changes as you go down Group 17 from fluorine to iodine.
Remember that $\text{Cl}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$, which is stronger than $\text{I}_2$.
Think about which halogen $\text{Br}^-$ can give electrons to, a stronger oxidiser above it or a weaker one below it.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Group 17 trend**

Oxidising power of the halogens decreases down the group. That means $\text{F}_2$ is strongest and $\text{I}_2$ is weakest.

Trend:
$$\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2 \text{ (oxidising agents)}$$

**Flip the trend for halide ions**

Reducing power of halide ions increases down the group. So $\text{I}^-$ is the strongest reducer and $\text{F}^-$ is the weakest.

Trend:
$$\text{I}^- > \text{Br}^- > \text{Cl}^- > \text{F}^- \text{ (reducing agents)}$$

**Apply to $\text{Br}^-$ ions**

A halogen higher up will oxidise a halide ion lower down. So $\text{Cl}_2$ (above) can oxidise $\text{Br}^-$, which means $\text{Br}^-$ reduces $\text{Cl}_2$.

$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{Br}_2$$

**Check $\text{Br}^-$ with $\text{I}_2$**

$\text{I}_2$ is below bromine, so it is too weak an oxidiser to take electrons from $\text{Br}^-$. No reaction occurs. This confirms the correct statement.

options.A: Correct. $\text{Cl}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$, so $\text{Br}^-$ can reduce it to $\text{Cl}^-$. $\text{I}_2$ is a weaker oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$, so $\text{Br}^-$ cannot reduce it. This matches the displacement rule that a more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive halide.
options.B: $\text{Cl}_2$ is above both bromine and iodine in the group, so it is a stronger oxidiser than both $\text{Br}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$. It will oxidise both $\text{Br}^-$ and $\text{I}^-$, not just $\text{Br}^-$. Choosing this suggests forgetting that $\text{I}^-$ is even easier to oxidise than $\text{Br}^-$.
options.C: This reverses the trend. $\text{F}_2$ is the strongest oxidising agent of the four because fluorine is the most electronegative and most readily gains electrons. $\text{I}_2$ is the weakest oxidising agent.
options.D: This also reverses the trend. $\text{I}^-$ is the strongest reducing agent because its outer electron is furthest from the nucleus and most easily lost. $\text{F}^-$ is the weakest reducing agent as it holds its electrons most tightly.
